highlights.quote: some pre-workout supplements contain more than 12 times as much caffeine per fluid ounce
highlights.note: Twelve times coffee, per ounce. I take pre-workout three times a week and have never once checked the label.

highlights.quote: these products do not go through the same premarket safety testing required for medications
highlights.note: Why does a drink with this much stimulant count as food? Who decided that, and when?

highlights.quote: Cardiac arrest was reported about 11 times more often
highlights.note: Big number, but it's eleven times more often in the reports, not eleven times more likely to happen to you.

highlights.quote: it is unknown how many people consumed these products without experiencing any cardiac events
highlights.note: This is the paragraph that should have been near the top.

highlights.quote: Cardiac arrest was reported about 11 times more often
highlights.note: These are voluntary reports. People report what they already suspect, so energy drinks were always going to show up.

highlights.quote: sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk
highlights.note: Where something sits on the shelf as a signal that it's safe. Never thought of the shelf as a message.

highlights.quote: consuming them before intense exercise or mixing them with alcohol or drugs
highlights.note: I'd like to know how many of the reports involved alcohol. That might be the real story.

highlights.quote: health care professionals should remember to ask their younger patients
highlights.note: Sending this to my sister. She's an ER nurse.

reflections.prompt: What surprised you most in this piece?
reflections.answer: How much of the finding rests on people choosing to file a report.

leftQuestions: Has anyone here cut back on energy drinks, and did you notice a difference?

highlights.quote: Sales of caffeinated energy drinks have more than doubled over the past decade
highlights.note: Doubled in ten years. That matches every gas station fridge I walk past.

highlights.quote: consuming up to 400 mg of caffeine per day
highlights.note: Look up how much is in the cans I actually drink.

highlights.quote: sold next to soda and bottled water, so most people assume they carry no real risk
highlights.note: This is exactly me. I've never thought of them as different from a soda.

highlights.quote: the study does not prove that caffeine products cause these events
highlights.note: So what would it take to prove it? A trial sounds impossible to run ethically.

reflections.prompt: What would you want to ask someone else who read it?
reflections.answer: Whether they'd change anything about what they drink after reading it.

highlights.quote: actually found heme inside a fossil blood cell ever
highlights.note: 115 million years and the chemistry is still in there.

highlights.quote: no-one is cloning dinosaurs anytime soon
highlights.note: Glad the writer answered the question everyone was thinking.

highlights.quote: What we found is that the bone was almost 80 per cent heme.
highlights.note: Eighty percent? How is a bone mostly a blood molecule? I feel like I'm misreading this.

highlights.quote: They are currently running tests on whether they can mineralise human blood with mat samples from Shark Bay.
highlights.note: I want to see how this experiment turns out.

highlights.quote: But some experts were yet to be convinced the ellipsoid shapes seen in the study were definitively blood cells.
highlights.note: Good that the sceptics get real space in the piece.

highlights.quote: This is smaller than almost all non-mammalian red blood cells, which are larger because of the retained nucleus
highlights.note: Is size alone enough to rule it out? Couldn't cells shrink as they mineralise?

highlights.quote: What we found is that the bone was almost 80 per cent heme.
highlights.note: Hard to square with how cautious the other scientists are. I'd want to see the paper's own wording.

highlights.quote: We'll be able to completely ask new questions of these fossils that have been in museums for decades
highlights.note: Old fossils sitting in drawers turning into new evidence. Lovely idea.

reflections.prompt: What surprised you most in this piece?
reflections.answer: That the experts quoted disagree so openly in the same article.

leftQuestions: Does anyone know how scientists tell a fossil cell apart from a mineral that just looks like one?

highlights.quote: Coastal microbes you would find at the beach may have helped preserve red blood cells
highlights.note: The beach microbes are the quiet heroes of this story.

highlights.quote: It died on microbial mats, colonies of bacteria and archaea often found in coastal locations.
highlights.note: Read up on microbial mats. Are these the same as the stromatolites at Shark Bay?

highlights.quote: We are not talking about intact blood cells or preserved haemoglobin, but rather chemical remnants
highlights.note: This sentence is the actual claim. Headlines say blood cells; the scientist says remnants.

highlights.quote: the conventional wisdom that organic material disappeared after a million years or less was now being routinely challenged
highlights.note: When did this shift start? Was it Schweitzer's T. rex work?

highlights.quote: 100 billion times smaller than an atom
highlights.note: I can't picture this at all. Is there any comparison that helps?

highlights.quote: exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second
highlights.note: Detecting something that lives that briefly is amazing to me.

highlights.quote: Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter
highlights.note: Which theories? The article doesn't say.

highlights.quote: I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad
highlights.note: The human side, tucked into the middle of a physics story.

reflections.prompt: What surprised you most in this piece?
reflections.answer: The funding story ended up more interesting to me than the physics.

highlights.quote: A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.
highlights.note: Feels like a coined word to make the result sound bigger. Would physicists really say this?

highlights.quote: Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter
highlights.note: "Some theories" is carrying the whole headline.

highlights.quote: the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product
highlights.note: People as the real product of research, not papers. Good way to put it.

highlights.quote: there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support
highlights.note: The standard answer, but probably also true.

leftQuestions: Is there a good explainer on what a beauty quark actually is?

highlights.quote: smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them
highlights.note: A clear explanation for someone like me who skipped physics.

highlights.quote: Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter
highlights.note: If dark matter only shows up through gravity, why would a quark breaking down tell us anything about it?

highlights.quote: I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad
highlights.note: How many researchers have already left? Is there data on this?

highlights.quote: The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.
highlights.note: Where did the record money go, then?
